title: Household measures and temperature
blurb: Turn teaspoons, tablespoons, fluid ounces and cups into milliliters, and convert temperatures between Celsius and Fahrenheit in the right order.
question: A 4 fl oz bottle of children's medicine is dosed at 1.5 tsp three times a day, and the child's temperature reads 39 °C. How many full days will the bottle last, and what is the temperature in °F?

teach.body: Formally, household measures are the teaspoon, tablespoon, fluid ounce and cup, each given a standard metric equivalent for labeling (1 tsp = 5 mL, 1 tbsp = 15 mL). In plain English: medicine labels, recipes and intake charts mix spoons, cups and milliliters, and you need to move between them in one or two steps. Learn the spoon and fluid-ounce values by heart; a cup is usually given to you as 240 mL.

head: Household
Customary
Metric
teach.caption: The values agree with each other: 3 × 5 mL = 15 mL; 2 × 15 mL = 30 mL; 8 × 30 mL = 240 mL.

teach.h: Worked household conversions (each checked both ways)
items: 2 tsp to mL: 2 × 5 = 10 mL. Check: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 tsp.
45 mL to tbsp: 45 ÷ 15 = 3 tbsp. Check: 3 × 15 = 45 mL.
6 fl oz to mL: 6 × 30 = 180 mL. Check: 180 ÷ 30 = 6 fl oz.
1.5 cups to mL (1 cup = 240 mL): 1.5 × 240 = 360 mL. Check: 360 ÷ 240 = 1.5 cups.

teach.body: Celsius to Fahrenheit: °F = (9/5 × °C) + 32. Multiply first, then add 32. Fahrenheit to Celsius: °C = (°F - 32) × 5/9. Subtract 32 first, then multiply. On a basic calculator, 9/5 is 1.8: multiply by 1.8 going up to °F. Going down to °C, multiply by 5 and divide by 9. The order matters because each formula undoes the other in reverse.

teach.caption: Kelvin, if you meet it: K = °C + 273.

head: Celsius
Fahrenheit
Note
teach.caption: Use these to sense-check: any reading above 0 °C must be above 32 °F.

teach.h: Celsius readings with their Fahrenheit partners
Scenario: Jasmine reads a medicine label
teach.body: Jasmine, a nursing applicant, helps her neighbor with a 4 fl oz bottle of children's medicine dosed at 1.5 tsp three times a day. Bottle: 4 × 30 = 120 mL. Dose: 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 mL. Per day: 7.5 × 3 = 22.5 mL. 120 ÷ 22.5 = 5.33, so it lasts 5 full days. The child's temperature is 39 °C: 39 × 1.8 = 70.2, plus 32 = 102.2 °F.

teach.text: The temperature traps: forgetting the 32, adding 32 before multiplying (°C to °F), or multiplying before subtracting 32 (°F to °C). The spoon traps: using 15 mL for a teaspoon or 5 mL for a tablespoon, and treating a cup as 16 fl oz.

items: 1 tsp = 5 mL; 1 tbsp = 3 tsp = 15 mL; 1 fl oz = 2 tbsp = 30 mL; 1 cup = 8 fl oz (240 mL when given).
For supply questions (how many full days or doses), round DOWN.

summary: You can now convert teaspoons, tablespoons, fluid ounces and cups to milliliters and back, and work out how long a supply lasts. You can also convert any temperature between Celsius and Fahrenheit by doing the steps in the correct order.

A.q: Directions on a bottle say to take 2.5 tsp of liquid medicine. How many milliliters is this?

whyNot.0: This uses 15 mL, which is a tablespoon, not a teaspoon.
whyNot.1: This multiplies by 3, the number of teaspoons in a tablespoon.
whyNot.3: This divides by 5 instead of multiplying.

A.q: A patient's temperature is 38 °C. What is the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?

whyNot.1: This multiplies by 1.8 but forgets to add 32.

A.q: A recipe calls for 6 tbsp of oil. How many fluid ounces is this?
A.why: 2 tbsp = 1 fl oz, and tablespoons are the smaller unit, so divide: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 fl oz.

whyNot.0: This divides by 3, the teaspoons-per-tablespoon factor.
whyNot.2: This multiplies by 2 instead of dividing.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 3, which would give teaspoons.

B.q: A thermometer reads 102.2 °F. What is this temperature in degrees Celsius?

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 5/9 without subtracting 32 first.
whyNot.1: This multiplies by 5/9 first and subtracts 32 afterward: the steps are in the wrong order.
whyNot.2: This subtracts 32 but then multiplies by 9/5 instead of 5/9.

B.q: Using 1 cup = 240 mL, a patient drinks 1.5 cups of tea, 2 fl oz of juice and 4 tbsp of broth. What is the total intake in milliliters?

whyNot.0: This uses 5 mL per tablespoon for the broth (20 mL instead of 60 mL).
whyNot.1: This uses 15 mL per fluid ounce for the juice (30 mL instead of 60 mL).
whyNot.3: This uses 30 mL per tablespoon for the broth (120 mL instead of 60 mL).

B.q: Which pair shows the same temperature on both scales?

whyNot.3: This adds 32 before multiplying: (10 + 32) × 1.8. In fact 10 °C = 50 °F.

C.q: A bottle holds 4 fl oz of medicine. The dose is 1.5 tsp three times a day. How many full days will the bottle last?
C.why: Bottle: 4 × 30 = 120 mL. Each dose: 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 mL. Per day: 7.5 × 3 = 22.5 mL. 120 ÷ 22.5 = 5.33, so 5 full days.

whyNot.0: This rounds 5.33 up. The sixth day would run short, so only 5 full days are covered.
whyNot.2: 16 is the number of doses (120 ÷ 7.5), not days.
whyNot.3: This uses 15 mL per fluid ounce, so the bottle looks like only 60 mL.

C.q: A patient's temperature rises from 98.6 °F to 101.3 °F. What is the new temperature in degrees Celsius?

whyNot.0: This adds the 2.7 degree Fahrenheit rise straight onto 37 °C; Fahrenheit and Celsius degrees are different sizes.
whyNot.2: This multiplies by 5/9 first and then subtracts 32.

C.q: Using 1 cup = 240 mL, one batch of a recipe needs 3/4 cup of milk. Nina makes 2.5 batches and has only a tablespoon to measure with. How many tablespoons of milk does she need?
C.why: 3/4 cup = 0.75 × 240 = 180 mL per batch. 180 × 2.5 = 450 mL. 450 ÷ 15 = 30 tbsp. Check: 1 cup = 16 tbsp, so 3/4 cup = 12 tbsp, and 12 × 2.5 = 30.

whyNot.0: 12 tbsp is the amount for one batch, not 2.5 batches.
whyNot.1: This divides 450 mL by 5, which counts teaspoons.
whyNot.3: This divides 450 mL by 30, which counts fluid ounces.

reteach.title: Think of a thermostat with two dials
reteach.question: Picture a thermostat whose two dials are labeled differently but always point to the same temperature. Why do you need two steps, in a set order, to read one dial from the other?

blocks.h: Different starting points, different step sizes
blocks.body: The Fahrenheit dial starts its count 32 degrees higher (water freezes at 32 °F, not 0) and its degrees are smaller: 9 Fahrenheit degrees fit into every 5 Celsius degrees. So to read °F from °C, stretch by 9/5, then shift up 32. To go back, undo in reverse: shift down 32 first, then shrink by 5/9. Like getting dressed and undressed, the last step on the way in is the first step on the way out.

blocks.text: If your Celsius answer is bigger than the Fahrenheit reading you started with (for anything above -40), you skipped or misplaced the 32.

explain.body: 1 tsp = 5 mL and 1 tbsp = 15 mL (3 tsp). Milliliters to teaspoons: divide by 5.

test.q: How many teaspoons are in 45 mL?

whyNot.2: This divides by 3, which is not a milliliter factor.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 5 instead of dividing.

explain.body: 1 fl oz = 2 tbsp = 30 mL, and 1 cup = 8 fl oz. The cup's metric value (240 mL) is given in the question when you need it.

whyNot.0: This uses 15 mL, which is a tablespoon.
whyNot.2: This uses 5 mL, which is a teaspoon.
whyNot.3: This uses 240 mL, which is a whole cup, for each fluid ounce.

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 1.8 but forgets to add 32.
whyNot.1: This adds 32 but skips the multiplication by 9/5.
whyNot.2: This uses the °F to °C formula on a Celsius reading.

explain.body: Subtract 32 FIRST, then multiply by 5/9. 77 °F: 77 - 32 = 45, and 45 × 5 ÷ 9 = 25 °C.

whyNot.1: This subtracts 32 but then multiplies by 9/5 instead of 5/9.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 5/9 first and then subtracts 32.
